The product's differentiator is visual and it worked for ten years: PR_DESIGN 460 (25.77%, 4.33★, 2016 → 2026), the single largest theme; with the per-habit cover photo (PR_PHOTOS 97, 5.43%) the visual union is 523 (29.30%, 4.36★); reviewers treat it as the mechanism, not decoration — 'I'm a very visual person, so the combination of large pictures and colourful calendars/graphs is great. I really feel motivated to tick things off, more than any other habit app' (4★); custom backgrounds named as the one reason productivity improved most across 15 trackers in three years; 'It sets a craving, when I see the image, I want to accomplish the goal'; paired with simplicity (PR_SIMPLE 361, 20.22%, 4.68★) this is what 'best in category' rests on — PR_BEST 204 (11.43%), 4.78★, the highest mean of any large theme.

The second differentiator — 'cards' — is loved by a minority and ignored by most: PR_CARDS 70 (3.92%, 4.69★), the depth union 192 (10.76%, 4.72★) — what power users name when explaining why they chose Today over a prettier-but-thinner rival ('the deciding factor was the extensibility of supplementary information via cards', jp 5★, running it alongside Momentum and Habity); but the corpus's most specific negative is NEG_FEATURE_UNUSED 15 (0.84%, 2.80★) — 'cards that are unusable in 95% cases'; 'those cards aren't really needed'; 'photos per habit are more of a gimmick at first' — and UX_CONFUSE 74 (4.15%) cannot work out the custom chart, counter or milestone card; 'the cards are simultaneously the reason power users pay and a source of confusion for everyone else'.

A performance bug that scales with success: the app slows in proportion to accumulated check-ins — BUG_PERF 70 (3.92%), 0.74% of E1 → 16.95% of E5; 'it takes about 5 seconds to register, if I'm registering a long streak of 50 day's or so, which is how I've been using it for 3 years, it takes so long I've stopped bothering' (gb 1★); 'past 1,000 days a single tap means a mysterious freeze then a crash' (jp 1★); '200 check-ins is not really a large amount of data; the storage must be inefficiently programmed' (de 3★); 'It can take over a minute from when you mark something as done… I've contacted support multiple times over the past 6 months' (1★); 'a habit tracker that punishes long streaks with latency drives away exactly the users who proved the product works' — 17 of the 70 also record leaving, being blocked or threatening to leave.

The Apple Watch app was requested for 14 months, shipped and never worked properly: REQ_WATCH 34 (1.90%) from 2016-03-11; shipped ~May 2017; from then BUG_WATCH 88 (4.93%, 2.98★) vs 21 praising it — check-ins revert ('several check ins I did earlier had reverted to not done'; 'I tap an icon to say I've done it, then 20 minutes late it's unchecked again!!'), phone and watch disagree, the complication is unavailable on most watch faces ('there is only one watch face that'll work with this app'); requests for Infograph complications (2018) recur for seven years, never answered.

The visual model — beauty is functional for a habit app because it makes you want to open it: 'because the design is beautiful, motivation rises easily — a surprisingly important point' (jp 4★); 'So beautiful that it makes me want to just do the items so I can click them off'; 'if it isn't all there in front of me in an endearing way, then I slack off and say NOPE'; 'It changes habit tracking from a chore into a fun experience I enjoy and look forward to'; a Good Design Award recipient in broadcast graphics: 'one of the most thoughtfully designed apps I have used' (2026).

§8.1 immediate fix — make check-in latency independent of history size: write latency grows with accumulated check-ins (diagnosed at ~200, total failure past 1,000, 5 seconds per tap after three years, over a minute); 24.3% of those reviewers also record leaving or being blocked; 'the highest-leverage fix in the report because of who it hits: the users with the longest histories are the ones who proved the product works, are most likely to have paid, and are most likely to be publicly enthusiastic'; 'test it the way users experience it: seed 20 habits × 1,000 check-ins and measure tap-to-confirmation. Do not test on a fresh install.'

§8.4 immediate fix — never lose data, and never lose it from a paid backup: 12 of 55 data-loss reviewers had paid and backup is the paid feature (a wiped three-year history; a backup overwritten by the restore flow; 'lost ALL my information on 2 occasions'); minimum bar: restore must never destroy the backup it is reading, a failed restore must leave existing data intact, covers/photos must survive a restore; the right shape is probably optional account-based sync — not mandatory, because on-device data is something reviewers actively praise.

§8.5 immediate fix — ship the iOS home-screen widget: REQ_WIDGET 47, the only request that grows as the corpus shrinks (1.98% → 16.95%), home-screen requests 2020-09 → 2025-12; conversion evidence is unusually direct — 'they urgently need a widget and I swear I'd pay premium'; 'its lack of a widget means I'll probably need to look for something else'; the NC widget's history proves the value: the primary interface when it existed (PR_WIDGET 28, 4.50★), 11 complaints in six languages when it vanished for two months.

§8.6 experiment — let a habit be paused, archived or legitimately skipped: REQ_ARCHIVE 11 + REQ_SKIP 11, the corpus's most-upvoted request; 'the current design forces a user who has succeeded to delete their habit and destroy the record of succeeding. That is a strange thing for a habit app to do'; two needs — archive ('already formed or no longer needed, but currently you can only delete it') and skip (illness, travel, 'a bad mental-health day' — one uses it to manage depressive episodes and calls it the reason the app worked); a skip feature already exists and nobody understands it — three ask what it does and one reports it damaging streak statistics: 'fixing the explanation may be worth more than building anything'.

§8.7 experiment — resolve the 'bad habits' promise: the listing says 'Quit bad habits and stay on track' and the product cannot track a limit (REQ_BREAKBAD 15, USE_QUIT 16 trying anyway); two honest options — build a 'maximum N per period' habit type as five reviewers describe and as Done and HabitBull are named as having, or remove the promise; 'what is not defensible is the current state: advertising a capability, collecting users who need it, and having them discover the gap after purchase'.

§8.8 experiment — give the one-page-per-habit model an escape hatch: REQ_DASHBOARD 70 (ten years), BUG_SWIPE 39, UX_FRICTION 41; 'the full-screen-photo model is the differentiator and the scaling problem. Do not remove it; make it optional past a threshold' — users have specified the fix: 'list as a default view; tap on an item will add a point; a habit image as a part of a row'; 'I want the task list shown on launch' (jp); 'the ability to not use a picture for every habit but rather just a simply background to make the app faster' (1★ — connecting the visual model to the performance problem).

§8.9 experiment — re-examine the free tier with the corpus's own evidence: 1 habit → MON_FREE1 78 at 1.97★ (71 in 2016 alone; the complaint returned within months of the cap being restored ~2022); 3 habits → MON_FREE3 67 at 3.60★, the same grievance 1.63 stars higher; 3–5 habits → zero one-habit complaints in four years; MON_TRIAL_REQ 33 made identically in 2016 and 2024 — 'one habit is not a trial, it is a screenshot. A one-habit cap in an app whose paid value is multi-habit dashboards prevents the prospect from ever seeing the thing they would be buying'; caveat: the 1★ at a 1-habit cap come disproportionately from people who never used the app — removing them may raise the rating without raising revenue; §8.13 #1 A/B test with revenue, not rating, as the metric.

§8.10 immediate fix — the $299.99 tier needs an explanation or a change: $3.99/month, $9.99/year and $299.99 'All premium features' — 'why is Today Premium $10 per year, but ALL Premium Features are $300 ❓ what is the difference' (2★); 30× the annual price — 'whatever the intent — a lifetime tier, a price-anchoring device, a legacy artefact — it currently reads to users as either a mistake or contempt, and it sits next to a history of paying customers losing their purchase'; MON_SUBSCRIPTION 8, all post-2022, none positive, vs PR_ONETIME 23 at 4.61★ praising the replaced model.

§8.11 immediate fix — answer support, and be seen to: SUP_NORESP 25 vs PR_DEV 39 (30 of 39 pre-2019), FIX_CONFIRM 33 (21 pre-2019); repeated documented instances of a reply converting a 1★ into a 5★; the in-app support email address is misspelled (toda@neybox.com) and the corrected one got no reply — 'the cheapest fix in this report'. §8.12 copy: the full-screen personal photo per habit (the single most-credited mechanism), a per-habit configurable dashboard (PR_CARDS 4.69★), one-time pricing honestly priced (4.61★), visible responsiveness (a rollback earning public rating upgrades), no ads / no account / on-device data; do not copy: one screen per habit as the only navigation, selling backup then losing data, gating the biometric lock then shipping a build where enabling it crashes, a visual design whose data layer scales worse than the visuals, advertising a capability you do not have, letting an unlaunchable build sit for 1,030 days — 'what converts a category-leading app into abandonware'.

Users managing depression use the skip mechanic as a mental-health tool: 'I started using this app to get a better grip on my depressive phases, and to sort days when I felt bad out of the streak. Over time it became easier to assess my successes' (de 5★) — the corpus's most substantive account of the app as a mental-health aid; the same skip feature is misunderstood by others (three ask what it does) — a forgiving state matters most to the people who need it most.

The two models stated verbatim: 'Usage-cap (taster) model: Free users can do everything core to the app but only a fixed amount (e.g. up to N tasks). This helps users build habits on full functionality and upgrade once they max out usage.' and 'Feature-gate (split) model: Free users get all usage they need but some valuable features (analytics, multi-device sync, admin controls) require payment. This is effective in team apps where paid features have clear ROI.' Many leading SaaS products run a hybrid: generous or unlimited core usage plus limited basic services, with advanced or business-oriented features premium-only.

Capability gates draw less immediate backlash than quantity gates because 'users expect to purchase non-essential extras (custom themes, widgets, advanced stats) once they've already invested time.' The sequencing matters as much as the object: the expectation forms after the time investment, not at install.

The capabilities habit apps commonly gate, as named: Apple Watch support, widget access, detailed analytics, and backup/sync. A Zapier review of free project managers is cited for the complementary pattern — unlimited tasks and collaborative features on a free plan create strong adoption, while premium plans monetise cloud sync and reporting.

Habit-formation timing is the reason a habit app's paywall cannot be early: habit-formation research puts the average at about 66 days for a new habit to become automatic, so 'if a habit app slams a limit or trial around day 7-14, users quit before they've truly engaged.' A truly free core — unlimited habits/tasks, reliable reminders, no lockouts — lets the routine form first; only afterwards do users become sensitive to missing extras, which is when they will pay to enhance an app that is already valuable.

The document's conclusion, stated as a rule: 'don't cripple the core habit/task loop in free tiers.' Free users should create and track unlimited or many habits/tasks; monetisation comes from capability gates — advanced analytics, custom themes, widgets, device sync/backup and similar enhancements. The named mechanism is trust: preserving unlimited core use builds the retention and trust that make an engaged user willing to pay later, whereas strict quantity limits make the free plan 'feel like a trick' — "'free' feels misleading if you can only log 3 tasks." Leading freemium designers are cited for protecting a free-user 'bill of rights' — unlimited logging, streaks, reminders — and gating only non-essential add-ons. The document answers its own question directly: 'Yes, the claim is supported by evidence', and names the model 'capabilities not quotas'.

The generic 'quit anything' market has one incumbent and a graveyard behind it. US ratings (verbatim): App | US ratings ; Days Since: Quit Habit Tracker | 19,073 ; Quitzilla: Quit Tracker | 1,473 ; Quit Bad Habits & Addiction | 1,061 ; Days Without: Break Bad Habits | 6 ; ZeroBadHabits | 0 — 'One app has traction. The rest are near zero. That is not a market with room in it.' The ceiling on the category leader is ~19k US ratings.

The money in quitting is in verticals, not in 'quit anything'. US ratings (verbatim): App | US ratings ; I Am Sober | 186,328 ; Smoke Free | 57,263 ; Reframe: Drink Less | 44,339 ; Sober Time | 41,632 ; Nomo — Sobriety Clocks | 16,398 ; QuitNow! | 13,572 — 'These beat every generic quit app by 3-10x.' The stated reason is search intent plus content: someone quitting smoking searches 'quit smoking', not 'quit tracker', and wants lung-recovery milestones, craving support and a community, 'none of which a generic counter provides'. The conclusion is that a generic quit app loses on both sides — too vague for the vertical searcher and redundant for the habit-tracker user.

Quit tracking is becoming table stakes inside habit trackers rather than a differentiator: 8 of the top 40 habit trackers explicitly market breaking bad habits — including Habit Tracker (#1), HabitKit, Streaks and Simple Streak — and 'the #1 app already ships a Quit tab'. The document states both halves plainly: 'Shipping it doesn't differentiate you. Not shipping it is starting to look like a gap.'

The #1 app's quit implementation fails in five named ways, quoted from its reviews: 'the streak counter is sometimes wrong for Quit habits'; 'It is not possible to track if you want to quit drinking alcohol. You can only choose a max period of 1 month with a 2 drink minimum?'; "When habits are set to 'Quit' with 0 per day — nothing is readable because of the all dark colors"; 'I click the QUIT habit tab, I get the form error'; 'Bad for quitting habits'. The document names this as the opportunity: 'The leader ships quit-habits badly. Doing it properly is a differentiator inside your existing app — and costs you nothing in downloads, because the traffic is already coming for habit tracking.'

The quit audience and the build-good-habits audience barely overlap: only 2.4% of Days Since reviewers ask for good-habit building, and 'Quit users mostly want one thing: a clean day counter that does not reset.' The document says this cuts both ways — a combined app will not cannibalise a quit app, but a separate quit app gains almost no cross-sell: 'Two apps, two ASO efforts, two support queues, for two groups that don't migrate.'

What people actually quit, from 10,621 Days Since reviews (verbatim): Category | Share of reviews ; Alcohol | 5.0% ; Smoking / vaping | 3.7% ; Social media / phone | 2.0% ; Sugar / junk food | 1.0% ; Weed / drugs | 0.7% ; Nail biting, caffeine, gambling | 0.6% ; Porn | 0.2%. The two largest categories are locked up by the verticals; social media and phone use are not — 'no large dedicated app owns it, and it's the third-biggest quit reason. That's the one quit niche with genuine room.'

A quit habit needs a days-since counter, not a streak: 'Quitting is days clean, not did it today.' The two mechanics are different data models and the document names the counter as the first-class requirement for the habit type.

A relapse must not wipe history — 'the most-repeated complaint in the Days Since corpus' (10,621 reviews). The specified behaviour is to log the slip, keep the record, and show best-ever alongside current. This is the single most-repeated item in the leading quit tracker's corpus, so it is the defining failure mode of the category.

Quit goals need allowances, not only zero: "'2 drinks a week' is a real goal; the leader caps at one month and users complain loudly about it." The #1 app's ceiling of a one-month maximum period with a two-drink minimum is quoted in §4 as a blocking limitation for alcohol tracking.

Milestones carry the emotional payload of a quit tracker: 1/7/30/90 days plus money saved, and "Days Since's happiest reviews (4.77 average) are milestone screenshots" — the highest-rated behaviour in the leading quit corpus is a user photographing a milestone, which makes the milestone screen both the retention moment and the sharing surface.

Quit mode must be readable in dark mode — 'a literal, fixable complaint about the #1 app', whose quit habits set to 0 per day render as 'nothing is readable because of the all dark colors'. A contrast defect specific to the zero-target state of a quit habit.

Quit terms are a keyword surface a habit app can annex without a second listing: Days Since ranks #3 overall in the category on ranking strength and #1 in 10 rich markets 'purely on quit terms'. Adding a proper quit mode lets one listing compete for 'quit habit', 'break bad habits' and 'sobriety tracker' alongside the habit keywords, 'without splitting your ASO across two listings.'
